abstract: Background: The transition from fetal to postnatal circulation requires closure of the ductus arteriosus (DA), involving smooth muscle cell contraction followed by anatomical remodeling. However, the spatial organization and developmental transcriptional dynamics of vascular wall cells during this transition remain poorly understood. Methods: We analyzed vascular morphology and spatial transcript profiles of the mouse DA and aorta at five stages from embryonic day 14.5 (E14.5) to postnatal day 2.5 (P2.5), enabling paired comparisons within tissue sections. Selected findings were compared with an independent mouse single-cell RNA-sequencing dataset. Histological and spatial transcript analyses were also performed on human DA tissue and the adjacent pulmonary artery. Results: The DA exhibited transiently higher cell-cycle-associated transcription across multiple vascular wall populations at E16.5, preceding medial thickening at E18.5 and postnatal luminal closure. Prenatally, DA mural cells exhibited greater contractile-associated gene expression than aortic mural cells. This difference diminished after birth, accompanied by a marked shift toward synthetic-like transcriptional programs associated with extracellular matrix remodeling and proteolysis. Ductal endothelial cells exhibited postnatal divergence from aortic endothelial cells in matrix- and adhesion-associated gene expression. Adventitial fibroblasts displayed distinct extracellular matrix- and insulin-like growth factor-associated expression profiles. In a human postnatal DA specimen, synthetic-like mural cells were enriched in regions of disrupted elastic lamellae and prominent collagen staining and shared selected remodeling-associated markers with postnatal mouse DA mural cells. Conclusions: DA development and closure involve temporally organized transcriptional changes across vascular wall populations, characterized by prenatal cell-cycle-associated activity and rapid postnatal reorganization of mural transcriptional programs. These findings provide a spatial framework for understanding vascular cell plasticity and multicellular remodeling during DA closure.
